setupSteps: Attach the rope to the low pulley (near the floor). Choose a light weight; use the pin to set the weight stack and push it fully into the hole.
Pick up the rope with both hands, palms facing each other (neutral grip), and face away from the machine.

Stance. Take a staggered stance (one foot a half step forward, knees soft) for balance, or feet about hip-width with a slight hip hinge; sources differ, FitPlate prefers the staggered stance for beginners.

Raise the rope overhead with the hands behind the head, upper arms beside the ears, ribs down, chest tall, and the cable running between or just behind the legs. Step forward slightly so the weight stack is lifted off its rest and there is tension at the bottom.
Camera. Stand side-on to the phone, with the cable not hiding the elbow.
Choose one dumbbell you can control for 10-12 strict reps. Start very light; the move needs good shoulder mobility.
Seat. Use a bench with back support if you have one (it reduces lower-back strain; Fitnessvolt, snippet); sit tall with feet flat. Standing is fine if you can keep the ribs down.
Grip. Hold the dumbbell with both hands under the top plate (the "diamond" grip) or one hand at a time; keep the wrists straight.
Start position. Press the dumbbell overhead with arms nearly straight (do not lock the elbows hard), upper arms beside the ears.
Camera. Side-on, 2.5 m away, shoulder, elbow and hip visible.

steps.title: Take the start position
steps.action: Raise the rope or dumbbell overhead so the arms are nearly straight and the upper arms are next to the ears.
steps.feel: Light stretch at the back of the upper arm; shoulders steady.
steps.visualCheck: Side: upper arms near vertical, elbows beside the ears, arms nearly straight; front: elbows the same width, not flared.

steps.title: Brace the trunk
steps.action: Ribs down, abs gently tight, hips still, knees soft, chest tall.
steps.feel: Stable trunk, no arch in the lower back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs not poking forward, ears over shoulders, no head thrust forward.

steps.title: Lower the weight
steps.action: Bend only the elbows and let the weight go back behind the head; the upper arms do not move.
steps.feel: Stretch along the back of the upper arm.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbows stay beside the ears, forearms drop behind the head, no forward lean.

steps.title: Reach the bottom
steps.action: Stop when the elbows are about 90 degrees or less and you feel a comfortable stretch; do not drop into a sharp or pinching position.
steps.breathing: Brief pause in the breath only; do not strain.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle about 90 degrees or less (est.), elbows still beside the ears.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Straighten the elbows to send the weight back overhead.
steps.feel: Back of the upper arm working.
steps.visualCheck: Side: the upper arms stay still; the weight travels in a smooth line.

steps.title: Finish at the top
steps.action: Straighten the arms to nearly straight, stopping short of a hard lock-out.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle about 160 degrees or more (est.); shoulders not rocking back.

steps.title: Reset
steps.action: Pause with the arms overhead, ribs down, then repeat.
steps.visualCheck: Side: trunk upright, elbows beside the ears.

steps.title: Finish the set
steps.action: After the last rep, bring the weight down with control: for the cable, step back toward the machine and let the weight stack settle gently; for the dumbbell, lower it to the thighs while seated, then to the floor.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back neutral, no dropped weights.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flaring out
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flaring out. Why: the shoulders and chest help and the triceps get less work (Bodybuilding.com, snippet). Fix: think "elbows toward the ears", lower the load, squeeze a light grip.

commonMistakes.title: Arching the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Arching the lower back. Why: loses a neutral spine and can cause back discomfort, often from limited shoulder reach (snippets). Fix: ribs down, abs braced, use a seated bench with back support, or lower the load.

commonMistakes.title: Too heavy a load
commonMistakes.text: Too heavy a load. Why: form breaks, range shortens, the shoulders and back take over (Healthline-linked and Garage Gym Reviews sources, snippets). Fix: reduce until every rep is strict with a 2-3 second lowering.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning forward and turning it into a half press (cable)
commonMistakes.text: Leaning forward and turning it into a half press (cable). Why: shortens the range and shifts load (coaching article, snippet). Fix: tall chest, slight hip hinge only, stagger the feet.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing the reps
commonMistakes.text: Rushing the reps. Why: less time under tension and more strain at the elbow (Myprotein, snippet). Fix: lower for 2-3 seconds, press for 1-2.

commonMistakes.title: Going past straight or locking out hard
commonMistakes.text: Going past straight or locking out hard. Why: shoulders rock back and the elbow joint takes the stress (Livestrong, snippet). Fix: stop just short of a hard lock-out.

commonMistakes.title: Head thrust forward
commonMistakes.text: Head thrust forward. Why: strains the neck and the shoulders. Fix: long neck, eyes forward.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the dumbbell or rope drop behind the head
commonMistakes.text: Letting the dumbbell or rope drop behind the head. Why: jerks the elbow and the shoulder. Fix: control the lowering and stop at a comfortable stretch.

commonMistakes.title: Forcing the overhead position with stiff shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Forcing the overhead position with stiff shoulders. Why: the position needs good shoulder mobility (several sources); a stiff shoulder compensates with the back. Fix: use the pushdown (Gym 37) or a seated bench, or reduce the range.

safetyNotes: Keep the load light enough to hold the elbows still. If the elbows flare, the back arches or the weight drops, it is too heavy.
Shoulder mobility. The overhead position needs good shoulder range; if you cannot raise the arms beside the ears without arching the back, use the pushdown (Gym 37) or reduce the range.

Elbow caution. Overhead triceps work stretches the long head and raises tendon tension; one blog cited an unverified study linking heavy overhead extensions to elbow bursa and tendon irritation (secondary source, not verified). Tendon pain at the back of the elbow is best managed by lowering the load and volume; see a clinician if pain lasts. Treat this as a plausible risk, not a proven one.
High blood pressure: avoid long breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure; arms overhead can feel more strenuous.
Cable handling: check the pin is fully in, keep the rope under control when you step back, do not let the stack slam; dumbbell: do not drop it behind the head and keep it away from your face.
Spotter: not needed for light loads; for heavy dumbbell sets ask someone to stand nearby and help take the weight, never to push it.
Gym etiquette: re-rack the rope and return the pin to its lowest weight, wipe the bench and handles, do not hog the cable station between sets, do not film other members.

The angle thresholds (160 and 90 degrees for the elbow, 140 degrees for the elbow-pinned shoulder angle), the lean limit (20 degrees), the 2 s minimum rep, and all sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: ExRx page for the overhead extension (searched, not returned), Mayo Clinic, Harvard Health or NSCA pages for this exercise; an EMG study comparing cable overhead extension with pushdown (only the Maeo 2022 hypertrophy trial was found, seen as summaries); an overhead-extension-specific professional-body prescription or Compendium code; a fixed cable stack or dumbbell weight; a peer-reviewed trial of overhead extension injury or elbow tendon risk (the one blog claim is unverified); condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, shoulder problems, obesity and PCOS; the primary ACOG page; a peer-reviewed trial of stance (staggered versus parallel) for the cable version.
